title: The trusted kernel, and the day it was wrong
objective: Classify the lines of an axiom report, say what a build, an axiom list, a kernel replay and a comparator run each establish, and complete the stamp each one earns.

segments.title: A green build, and then what

blocks.md: A green build feels like an answer. In Lean it is not one, and this lesson is about the gap: what each check actually looked at, what a proof quietly assumes, and what happened in 2026 when a checker itself was wrong.

choice.prompt: `#print axioms transfer_conserves` prints `[propext, Quot.sound]` {{run:RUN-lean-ledger}}. What does that say?

options.text: The proof is unsound, because it uses axioms.
options.why: Standard axioms are part of Lean's logic and are not a defect.

options.text: It uses only standard axioms of Lean's logic.
options.why: The reference manual names `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound` as the standard three, and this list is within them. [Validating a Lean Proof](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/ValidatingProofs/)
A `sorry` shows up as `sorryAx`.
Native computation shows up as an axiom with `_native` in its name.

choice.prompt: A file whose theorem ends in `sorry` is built. What exit code does the build return?

options.why: A `sorry` only warns, so the build goes through {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}.
A failed build would exit non-zero, and a `sorry` fails nothing.
A start-up failure would exit non-zero, and nothing failed to start.
The file is built; the unfinished proof is reported as a warning.

blocks.md:
A Lean proof is a term, and the kernel checks that the term has the type of the statement. The term may lean on assumptions that Lean does not prove: axioms. `#print axioms` lists every axiom a theorem depends on, following the dependencies all the way down. It re-checks nothing. It tells you what the proof assumes, and the assumptions fall into four kinds.

| Kind | The list shows | The stamp it earns |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | some of `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` | PROVED [P] · Lean 4.35.0 kernel · axioms listed |
| Unfinished | `sorryAx` | no [P]: "PROVED modulo k assumed lemmas", each lemma ASSUMED [A] |
| Native | a name containing `_native` | PROVED [P] · kernel + compiler |
| Custom | an axiom someone declared | no [P]: the axiom is carried as ASSUMED [A], like `sorryAx` |

Here are five theorems, one for each kind and one for a tactic that adds nothing. Read the code, then make your call before you look at what `#print axioms` says about the native one.

blocks.direction: Replay shows: five theorems, each followed by the axioms it depends on. Read each line for the kind of axiom it reports. The last two theorems state something false, and the proofs are still accepted as far as the build goes.

code.text:
-- standard: a proof by `omega`
theorem by_omega (x y : Int) (h : x ≤ y) : x - 1 < y := by omega
-- native: `native_decide` trusts the compiler
theorem big_native : (2^64 : Nat) % 7 = 2 := by native_decide
-- none: `decide` evaluates inside the kernel
theorem by_decide : (2^10 : Nat) % 7 = 2 := by decide
-- unfinished: `sorry`
theorem with_sorry : (1 : Nat) = 2 := by sorry
-- custom: a declared axiom
axiom cheat : False
theorem with_axiom : (1 : Nat) = 2 := cheat.elim

#print axioms by_omega
#print axioms big_native
#print axioms by_decide
#print axioms with_sorry
#print axioms with_axiom

tap.property: every theorem here depends only on standard axioms

call.prompt: `big_native` is closed by `native_decide`. What will `#print axioms big_native` list?

options.why: `native_decide` adds an axiom that is not one of the standard three.
There is no `sorry` in this proof.

options.text: An axiom named for native evaluation: the compiler was trusted
options.why: `native_decide` runs compiled code and records that trust as an axiom with `_native` in its name.
This axiom is generated by `native_decide`. Nobody declared it.

blocks.after: The list for `big_native` names a `_native` axiom {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}. `native_decide` does not ask the kernel to evaluate the claim; it runs compiled code and trusts it, so the stamp becomes PROVED [P] · kernel + compiler, and comparator's permitted list leaves it out. `decide` lists no axioms, because the kernel itself did the evaluation. `with_sorry` lists `sorryAx`, and `with_axiom` lists the axiom someone declared. Neither of those two earns a [P].

choice.prompt:
A receipt prints these lines. Which stamp does the line for `c` earn?

```text
'a' depends on axioms: [propext, Quot.sound]
'b' depends on axioms: [sorryAx]
'c' depends on axioms: [c._native.native_decide.ax_1_1]
```

options.why: That is the stamp for line `a`. A native axiom puts the compiler inside what you trust.
A non-standard axiom is not a counterexample. It changes what is trusted, not what is true.

options.text: No [P]: PROVED modulo one assumed lemma, carried as ASSUMED [A]
options.why: That is the row for `b`. Native evaluation is trusted, and it is not an unfinished proof.
The proof is complete, and the qualifier names the compiler as part of the trust.

blocks.md:
Three checks sound alike and are not. A **build** elaborates your files: it runs the tactics, and it reports errors. An **axiom list** says what the finished proof assumes. A **kernel replay** takes every declaration in the environment and checks it again, however it got there. The difference matters, because the elaborator is not the kernel.

Three specimens from recorded runs show the gaps:

- A file whose theorem ends in `sorry` builds with a warning, and its axiom list names `sorryAx` {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}. A green build is no verdict on a proof.
- On a project with three non-standard axioms, `lake check` rejects each of them, and its log still says the default kernel accepts the solution {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}. Those are two verdicts: the kernel accepted the proofs, and the axiom policy refused three assumptions. Read every line.
- A declaration added while kernel checking is switched off by the option `debug.skipKernelTC`, and the theorem `1 = 2` built on it, both build clean and list no axioms {{run:RUN-lean-skipkernel}}. The source stays out of this page on purpose. The option line is the point.

blocks.direction: Run: a project whose theorem `anything : 1 = 2` rests on a declaration added with `debug.skipKernelTC` set. The build and its axiom lines come first, then the replay. The declaration's source is withheld.

code.text:
lake build              # elaborates every module
leanchecker Probe       # replays every declaration through the kernel

call.prompt: The build is clean and `#print axioms` lists nothing for `anything : 1 = 2`. Is `1 = 2` proved?

options.text: Yes: the build is clean and no axioms are listed.
options.why: Both outputs come from an elaborator told to skip the kernel, so neither checked that declaration.
True, and still not something these outputs can show. Only a kernel replay rejects the declaration.

options.text: Can't tell without a kernel replay.
options.why: The replay checks every declaration again, whoever added it, and it rejects this one.

blocks.after: The replay rejects the declaration {{run:RUN-lean-skipkernel}}. A build reports what the elaborator did, an axiom list reports what a proof assumes, and neither asks the kernel again. Only a replay does. That is why a Lean claim carries the checker's name: a stamp is only as good as the check behind it.

choice.prompt: Which pairing of a check with what it establishes is right?

options.text: A kernel replay: every declaration in the environment was checked again, whoever added it.
options.why: That is what replay adds, and why it caught the declaration the build let through.
A `sorry` only warns, so the build stays green {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}.

options.text: An axiom list: the kernel re-checked every declaration.
options.why: It lists assumptions and re-checks nothing.

options.text: A comparator run: the proof meets the business requirement.
options.why: Comparator adds the pinned statement, and no checker reads a requirement.

segments.title: The day the kernel was wrong

blocks.md:
One kernel is one place to trust. Comparator can run several: `--paranoid` checks your solution with every checker the toolchain bundles, and on a solution like yours it takes seconds {{run:RUN-lean-comparator}}. Its longer sibling, `lake check --paranoid`, replays the whole environment and takes minutes on a fast machine, so this lesson names it and does not wait for it {{run:RUN-bwrap-lanes}}.

In July 2026 an AI-assisted Lean "disproof" of the Collatz conjecture was published from a pipeline that replayed proofs, checked axioms and ran a pinned second checker. Run the check on your own project, and make your call about that pipeline before you read what happened.

blocks.direction: Run: comparator on the pinned challenge and your solution, with every bundled checker switched on. Each checker prints its own verdict line.

tap.property: the pinned theorems are proved about the pinned definitions

call.prompt: A pipeline replayed proofs, checked axioms and ran a pinned second checker. Could it accept a proof of `False`?

options.why: It did: two bugs in two checkers, one of them a week out of date.
Checks can share a blind spot, and a pinned checker can lag a fix.

blocks.after: `--paranoid` runs 6 checkers {{run:RUN-lean-comparator}}, and they can share a flaw: lean4lean ports the reference logic for inductive types. A PROVED stamp names its checkers and their versions, and an advisory can reopen it.

blocks.title: The day the kernel was wrong
blocks.md: On 2026-07-25 a Lean "disproof" of the Collatz conjecture was published from a pipeline that replayed proofs, checked axioms and ran a pinned second checker, nanoda. On 2026-07-28 issue #14576 reduced it to a proof of `False` with no axioms, and the kernel was fixed the same day. The postmortem of 2026-08-01 found two bugs, chained: the official kernel "had a missing check in the nested inductive type support", and nanoda "did not verify the type name in a projection node". The repository "also passed a week-old version of nanoda". A third checker, lean4lean, shared the kernel's bug because its inductive types port the reference implementation. The advisory of 2026-08-02 says exploiting it "requires execution of a metaprogram within the Lean process", which is why `lake check` runs your build in a sandbox and replays an export of the result. Sources: [the postmortem](https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-8-1-postmortem-for-kernel-soundness-bug-14576/) and [the advisory](https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/08/02/1).

choice.prompt:
These lines come from `lake comparator --paranoid` on a project whose theorem lists only standard axioms {{run:RUN-lean-comparator}}. Complete the stamp: PROVED [P] · Lean 4.35.0 kernel · axioms listed · …

```text
Lean paranoid kernel accepts the solution
lean4lean kernel accepts the solution
nanoda kernel accepts the solution
con-leche kernel accepts the solution
con-ron kernel accepts the solution
Lean default kernel accepts the solution
```

options.why: Six lines name six checkers, and the stamp names how many accepted.
One line per checker, and the stamp counts them.

options.text: · 6 checkers, which cannot share a flaw
options.why: They can: lean4lean ports the reference logic for inductive types, as the kernel bug showed.
That qualifier is for a `_native` axiom, and none is listed here.

blocks.md:
**Assumed, and tested at every Lean Defence:** the Lean 4.35.0 kernel accepts only well-typed terms. That is SEAM-15, and it sits under every claim you mint in this stage. It is held, not cracked. If an advisory ever reopens it, the news reaches you as a note on your claims, never as a silent change to them.

**Say it back.** Retell the story in four sentences, without exploit detail: what the pipeline checked, what was wrong, why a second checker did not save it, and what the fix and the advisory changed. Nothing here is graded.

choice.prompt:
A receipt prints these lines. Which stamp does the line for `z` earn?

```text
'x' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'y' depends on axioms: [y._native.native_decide.ax_1_1]
'z' depends on axioms: [trustMe]
```

options.why: That is the stamp for line `x`. `trustMe` is not a standard axiom.
That is the stamp for line `y`. Nothing here was evaluated natively.

options.text: No [P]: the axiom `trustMe` is carried as ASSUMED [A]
options.why: A custom axiom is treated like `sorryAx`. The proof stands on a claim that nothing checked.
A custom axiom changes what is assumed. It does not show the statement false.

choice.prompt: Which statement about automation and axioms is right?

options.why: `decide` lists no axioms, because the kernel did the evaluation {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}.
An `omega` proof can still list `propext` and `Quot.sound` {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}.

options.text: `native_decide` adds nothing, because the kernel still checks the evaluation.
options.why: It adds an axiom with `_native` in its name {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}.

options.text: `grind` can add `Classical.choice`, and the stamp lists it.
options.why: A `grind` proof can list a third axiom that a manual proof of the same theorem does not {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}.

The real lanes could not be run on this machine. configs[] holds local emulations, each labeled; lanes{} lists, for each lane, what stands in for it, what was not tested and the owner action that completes it.

The pack is the whole-lab configuration of curriculum/S02-proof.md section 3. Its statements are copied verbatim from the S02 spec (pack/lab2/challenge/Challenge.lean, public). Its three solution files, Solution.lean (proofs of the seven whole-lab theorems), broken/Broken.lean and fixed/Fixed.lean, are complete proofs and are not published: they are reference solutions, which stay in a private place (spine section 11.1). inputs[] lists them by SHA-256 with the role "private fixture, not published", as it lists the eight rejected solutions that mutate.mjs makes from Solution.lean; private-fixtures.json holds the same values. Broken and Fixed import Solution, because lake check loads every default target into one environment and fails with "environment already contains" when two of them define the same name.

The recorded configurations ran while the three files and eight rejected solutions were still inside the pack folder: each docker-run.argv mounts scripts/spikes/W0-S06/pack at /pack and names /pack/lab2 and /pack/variants. They have since been moved out of the public tree. The harness now takes the three from --solutions DIR (mounted at /solutions) and has mutate.mjs make the rejected solutions from Solution.lean (mounted at /variants); mutate.mjs --solutions DIR --verify shows that the files the harness is given have the SHA-256 values in inputs[] and that the eight it makes are byte for byte the ones that ran. The files were last modified at 2026-10-24T12:52:41Z, before the first configuration started (2026-10-24T13:41:34Z), and the hashes in inputs[] are theirs: runs/RUN-bwrap-lanes/private-fixtures-provenance.txt lists each file's hash and modification time, read from the copies kept outside the repository, and the result of comparing the eight rejected solutions that mutate.mjs makes with the files that ran. The probe wrote no fixtures.sha256 then; a configuration recorded with the present harness carries one (hashes only), and open[] names any that used other files.

A side trial, scripts/spikes/W0-S06/collision-trial.sh, is kept in runs/RUN-bwrap-lanes/trial-module-collision/: two libraries whose root modules are both named SelfTransfer, as the S02 layout sketch has. Lake built one SelfTransfer.olean, from the first library, never built the second, and lake build and lake check both exited 0.
Every step records the 1-, 5- and 15-minute load average at its start. This is a shared host: its timings were taken under whatever load other jobs put on it, and they are not promises.

A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.
